title: Pogacar, Evenepoel among riders being investigated by police over running red light at level crossing
content:
An official investigation has been opened by the Belgian police into the two dozen riders who ran a red light at a railway level crossing during Sunday’s Tour of Flanders.

“Ignoring a red light at a level crossing is a fourth-degree offense, the most serious category under traffic law, which can have severe consequences,” said the East Flanders Public Prosecutor’s Office in a statement. “Such an offense poses serious risks to the safety of both the riders and third parties. Therefore, these infringements are severely punished.”

Potential punishments for a fourth-degree offence, the most serious in Belgian law, include a fine of up to €5,000 and a possible driving ban ranging from eight days to five years.

The incident occurred with 213 kilometres remaining in the race, splitting the peloton into two. Favourites such as world time trial champion Remco Evenepoel and eventual winner Tadej Pogacar were all amongst the 20 to 30 riders to continue past the sirens and flashing lights, which started only seconds before they arrived at the level crossing, with the bunch travelling at over 50kph.

“The offenders have since all been identified and an official report is currently being drawn up,” the prosecutor’s office added.

Several other contenders, including Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert, waited behind the level crossing once the barriers came down.

Race rules stipulate that all riders should obey level crossing instructions on the course, with the commissaires then responsible for deciding whether the disruption constitutes a race incident or requires a neutralisation.

On Sunday, they ordered the front half of the peloton to wait for those riders stuck behind the traffic lights. The breakaway, three minutes ahead, who did not skip the red light, were allowed to extend their lead.

Pogacar eventually won the race, known as the Ronde, by 34 seconds from Van der Poel after gapping him on the final ascent of the Oude Kwaremont. He was later yellow-carded for discarding his gloves outside a litter zone — had the riders who skipped the level crossing been given a yellow card, as the rulebook would allow the commissaires to do, he would have been disqualified.

“Suddenly three guys jump in the middle of the road and start waving to stop,” Pogacar said in his winners’ press conference. “How can you stop in one second? I think they could prevent this by stopping us before, no? Not 10 metres before the crossing. I was thinking: ‘Maybe it’s like some protesters or something crazy is going on.’”

Pogacar’s UAE Team Emirates has been contacted for comment.

In the past, riders have been immediately disqualified from races for running red lights at level crossings, with the key issue surrounding whether cyclists deliberately passed through the warning, or whether they were unable to stop. The size of the group involved in Sunday’s incident added to the complexity of the race commissaires’ job.

The prosecutors will decide on whether to bring a formal criminal charge based on their investigation at a later date, with the office emphasising in a statement that “such violations are unacceptable, even in a sporting context.”
